messages.author: 435d850b52986b55
messages.subject: unusual precision when penalizing priors to =c(0.01...)
parts:
We have experimented a set of penalized priors, however we notice something unusual precision see below in yellow.

Basically for model “mod3” the mean precision for group is way higher than the posterior mean of random effects when we use "pc.prec", param = c(0.01, .01))? If we penalize up to .7 seems to be reasonable, is there any particular explanation?

thank you very much


pc_prec

library(INLA)

## Loading required package: sp

## Loading required package: Matrix

## Warning: package 'Matrix' was built under R version 3.4.3

## This is INLA_17.06.20 built 2017-06-20 03:42:30 UTC.
## See www.r-inla.org/contact-us for how to get help.

## Gaussian --------------------------------------------------------------------
m <- 1e3
set.seed(123)
x <- rnorm(m)
group <- sample(seq(1,100), size = m, replace = T)

# Random effect
tau.v0 <- 0.25
set.seed(334455)
v <- rnorm(length(unique(group)), 0, sqrt(1/tau.v0))
vj <- v[group]

# y
tau <- 3
set.seed(334455)
b0 <- 5
beta1 <- 2
y <- rnorm(m, b0 + vj, 1/sqrt(tau))


# Models
mod1 <- inla(y ~ 1 + f(group, model="iid"),
             family = "gaussian",
             data = data.frame(y, x, group),
             control.predictor = list(compute = T))

prior2 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .01)))
mod2 <- inla(y ~ 1 + f(group, model = "iid", hyper = prior2),
             family = "gaussian",
             data = data.frame(y, x, group),
             control.predictor = list(compute = T))

prior3 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.01, .01)))
mod3 <- inla(y ~ 1 + f(group, model = "iid", hyper = prior3),
             family = "gaussian",
             data = data.frame(y, x, group),
             control.predictor = list(compute = T))

prior4 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.7, .01)))
mod4 <- inla(y ~ 1 + f(group, model = "iid", hyper = prior4),
             family = "gaussian",
             data = data.frame(y, x, group),
             control.predictor = list(compute = T))

# Posterior hyperparameters (precision)
round(mod1$summary.hyperpar[, 1:2], 4)

##                                           mean     sd
## Precision for the Gaussian observations 2.9802 0.1404
## Precision for group                     0.2233 0.0317

round(mod2$summary.hyperpar[, 1:2], 4)

##                                           mean     sd
## Precision for the Gaussian observations 2.9801 0.1404
## Precision for group                     0.2381 0.0321

round(mod3$summary.hyperpar[, 1:2], 4)

##                                           mean     sd
## Precision for the Gaussian observations 2.9127 0.1405
## Precision for group                     1.2301 0.0672

round(mod4$summary.hyperpar[, 1:2], 4)

##                                           mean     sd
## Precision for the Gaussian observations 2.9799 0.1403
## Precision for group                     0.2467 0.0324

# Posterior mean of random effects
preds <- data.frame(mod1 = mod1$summary.random$group$mean,
                    modd2 = mod2$summary.random$group$mean,
                    modd3 = mod3$summary.random$group$mean,
                    modd4 = mod4$summary.random$group$mean)
apply(preds, 2, function(x) 1 / (sd(x)^2)) # precision

##      mod1     mod2     mod3     mod4
## 0.2208747 0.2211303 0.2391298 0.2212810

# Real precision
1 / sd(vj)^2 # sample

## [1] 0.2389246

tau.v0 # population

## [1] 0.25

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] unusual precision when penalizing priors to =c(0.01...)
parts:
Hi,

To interpret the pc prior, I usually compute the prior median for sigma (marginal standard deviation), which is the 1/lambda*log(2).

# Your Models
prior2 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(1, .01)))

l = 1*log(0.5)/log(0.1)
giving 0.3
prior3 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.01, .01)))

l = 0.01*log(0.5)/log(0.01)
giving 0.0015

prior4 <- prior1 <-list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(0.7, .01)))
l = 0.7*log(0.5)/log(0.01)
giving 0.1

From this you can see that when the location parameter (prior median of sigma) is somewhere near the truth, you recover the truth. When it is very far away from the truth, you do not recover the truth. 

PS: Using the prior median to specify the prior, with param = c(prior.median, 0.5) is a choice I make personally. But I end up with the same prior distribution, usually, as people who prefer to specify the 0.01 quantile.

Kind regards,
Haakon
